title: Rewards that backfire
hookLine: children promised a prize for drawing later drew less on their own (Lepper and colleagues)

cards: A preschool classroom. On a table, a set of markers and good drawing paper. Children who already liked to draw get a turn.

Some are told beforehand: draw, and you'll win a certificate with a gold seal and a ribbon. Others just draw. Later, the markers come back out during free play, and this time nobody is promising anything.
Which children pick them up? The answer runs against an easy assumption about rewards, and it's today's word.

teach.b: First, the finding. Mark Lepper, David Greene and Richard Nisbett ran that study.

The children who had been promised the award, and got it, later spent less of their free time drawing than children who got no award, or got one by surprise. Something that had been play started to behave like work.
Second, the detail that matters. It wasn't the prize itself. Children who received the same certificate without expecting it didn't draw less.
The drop showed up in the children who drew in order to get the prize.
The researchers tested this as the overjustification idea: when there's an obvious outside reason for doing something, people may lose sight of the inside one. Third, the link to yesterday.

teach.h: THE REASON SLIDES TO THE BACK.
teach.b: In Deci and Ryan's terms, an expected reward can make an activity feel controlled, and the reason that was yours slides into the background. The study doesn't say every reward ruins everything.
It says a promised prize can quietly change why someone is doing a thing. Fourth, an older text.

In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna that his right is to the action, never to its fruits, and that the fruit should not be his motive. The Gita is speaking about duty and the self, not about markers.
But the two meet at one point: work done only for the prize can lose what made it worth doing.

how: People who take this research to heart often keep at least part of their practice free of goals, scores and sharing, so the reason for doing it stays their own.

o: a prize so small it feels like an insult to the winner
a promised prize that makes a loved activity feel like work
a reward handed out by surprise, after the work is done

games.q: inside rewards that backfire: tap the pairs.

s: the study shows any reward kills interest
children who got the award by surprise didn't draw less.
children who expected the prize later drew less on their own
they spent less free time drawing than the other children.
the Gita passage is about drawing and prizes
it speaks about duty and the self; the two only meet at one point.

games.q: you're a child in the study, promised a gold-seal certificate for drawing. later the markers come back, no prize offered. what did children like you tend to do?
o: draw less than the other children.
draw just the same as everyone else.
games.why: the children who drew for the expected award spent less free time drawing; the surprise-award children didn't drop.

practice: For this sit there's no goal to hit, no calm to earn, nothing to report afterward. If the mind starts keeping score, how am I doing, is this working, notice the scoreboard and set it down.
Two minutes, for their own sake, and nothing else.

wordCard.voice: Rewards that backfire. A promised prize can make a loved activity feel like work, so people do less of it once the prize is gone. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: no prize needed. Some things are worth doing just for the doing. That's a week, done.

sources.ref: Lepper, Greene & Nisbett, "Undermining children's intrinsic interest with extrinsic reward: A test of the 'overjustification' hypothesis"
